newsitem.title: USA: N. Korea agrees to continue peace talk planning.
newsitem.headline: N. Korea agrees to continue peace talk planning.

text.p: North Korea agreed to continue planning landmark Korean peninsula peace talks with the United States, South Korea and China after Tuesday's first round of discussions, U.S. and South Korean officials said.

There was "a very cosy and a very good atmosphere. We had very substantive talks today but nothing has been agreed upon," a South Korean official who spoke anonymously said after the day-long session. Later, the Americans hosted a reception.
The four parties will meet again on Wednesday.

The goal of these "talks about talks" was to set a date and agenda for launching substantive negotiations to replace the fraying 1950-53 Korean War armistice with a more permanent peace, presumably in a treaty.
If all this can be worked out this week, the substantive negotiations are expected to commence sometime in September.

According to South Korean spokesman Ji Won Suh, the four delegations decided nothing would be considered agreed until all aspects of their discussion were settled, so in principle the other official's comment was not necessarily negative.

Given North Korea's erratic history on peace talks, the fact that its delegation agreed to resume talks on Wednesday at Columbia University's School of International and Public Affairs had to be seen as a positive sign.

Throughout the day U.S. officials refused to discuss the substance of the talks with reporters. North Korean officials were not available for comment, and China's delegation only made brief remarks. Most information came from the South Koreans.
"So far so good," Chinese delegation head Chien Jian told reporters at the conclusion of the morning session.
Suh said North Korea expressed hope in the meeting that "these preliminary talks will result in a fruitful conclusion."

Lead delegate Kim Gye Gwan said Pyongyang agreed to attend because the four-party talks are "regarded positively to establish a sustainable peace scheme on the Korean peninsula," Suh reported from the closed-door session.

He said negotiators accepted, over North Korean objections, China's suggestion to deal first with the easier issues -- date, level of representation, venue for the substantive talks -- and leave the thornier topic of agenda for last.

Pyongyang argued that peace talks should not interfere in domestic affairs and that U.S. forces in South Korea should be on the agenda, Suh said. He interpreted this as blaming America for tensions on the heavily fortified Korean peninsula.

But a U.S. official rejected any suggestion of trouble, saying: "This meeting is a positive development. The fact of the matter is there is a whole history that has to be overcome ... bad feelings do exist," and that is precisely why these peace talks were proposed.
Washington and Seoul worked for months to persuade Pyongyang's isolated Stalinist regime to join the peace process proposed in 1996 by the U.S. and South Korean presidents.
North Korea finally agreed, but only after being promised million of dollars in U.S. and South Korean food aid.

Tuesday's meeting marked a watershed because it included China for the first time and was a step closer to actual negotiations. China is North Korea's ally and, with the United States and the two Koreas, a party to the armistice.

The talks opened one day after North Korea, in an apparent goodwill gesture, turned over the remains of four U.S. soldiers missing from the Korean War and as relief workers reported that a drought is compounding North Korea's severe food shortages.

A main obstacle to peace talks had been Pyongyang's demand for food to compensate for famine caused by two years of severe rains and a system that cannot meet the country's needs. Suh said the issue of food was not raised in the morning but may come up later.
